about: The last prayer of the communion rite, and the one with a knot in it. Quem is masculine: it cannot belong to mácula, the stain, which is feminine, nor to sacraménta, which is neuter and plural. It reaches back over both of them to me, five words earlier — let no stain of sins remain in me, whom the pure and holy sacraments have refreshed. Latin can do this because the endings hold; a language that has lost them cannot, and every translation has to choose. The prayer also asks for something oddly physical: that the Body and Blood cleave to the priest's viscera, the innermost parts, not to his soul.

s02.translation: May Thy Body, O Lord, which I have received, and the Blood which I have drunk, cleave to my inmost parts:

s03.translation: and grant that no stain of sins remain in me, whom pure and holy sacraments have refreshed:

s04.translation: Who livest and reignest for ever and ever. Amen.

s05.narrative: The priest washes and wipes his fingers and drinks the ablution, wipes his mouth and the chalice, folds the corporal, covers the chalice and sets it on the altar as before, and goes on with the Mass.

w001.function: The first of two subjects of “adhǽreat” (w010), and the verb stays singular for both: Body and Blood are counted as one thing received.

w008.function: Masculine, agreeing with “Sanguis” (w007) — the same relative in a different gender four words after the last one.

w009.function: Poto is the ordinary word for drinking, with none of the ceremony of the sentence around it.

w010.function: Ad and hæreo, to stick fast to; it governs the dative, as inhærére does in the second prayer before Communion.

w011.function: Dative after “adhǽreat” (w010). Víscera are the organs beneath the ribs, not the soul: the prayer asks for something physical.

w014.function: A bare imperative, with the semicolon after it holding open what is to be granted.

w017.function: Ablative after in — inside me. This is the word that “quem” (w022) will reach back to, across two nouns of the wrong gender.

w020.function: Scelus is a heavier word than peccátum: a crime, an outrage, not a fault.

w021.function: Subject of “remáneat” (w019), and feminine — which is why the masculine relative that follows cannot belong to it.

w022.function: Masculine, and neither of its neighbours is: not the feminine “mácula” (w021), not the neuter “sacraménta” (w027). It reaches back to “me” (w017) — in me, whom the sacraments have refreshed. The endings make the leap safe.

w026.function: Re and fácio, to make again; the word is used of a meal that restores a traveller, and that is the picture.

w027.function: Plural: the Body and the Blood, both just received, counted as two.

w031.function: The shortest of the endings in this part of the Mass: no Trinity named, no God in apposition — the prayer is nearly over and the Mass is going on.
